name: Hungary
tagline: Thermal baths beneath grand Habsburg boulevards, castle hills, sweet Tokaji wine, the wide plains of the puszta and a Danube capital that shines after dark.
cardDescription: A compact Central European country of Budapest's baths and bridges, wine regions, the great Lake Balaton and a proud, distinctive culture, at very fair prices.
metaDescription: A complete Hungary travel guide: the 10 best places to visit, Budapest, the Danube Bend, Eger, Lake Balaton, Tokaj and Pécs, food, thermal baths, when to go, transport and a two-week itinerary.

image.alt: Buda Castle above the Danube seen from the Széchenyi Chain Bridge

intro: Hungary lies in the Carpathian Basin in the heart of Europe, a landlocked country of about 9.5 million people, roughly the size of Portugal. Its language, Hungarian, is unrelated to its Slavic, Germanic and Romance neighbours, and its culture is distinctive, shaped by the Magyars who arrived in the 9th century, by Ottoman rule, by the Habsburg empire and by the Soviet era. It has been an EU member since 2004.

Most visitors come for Budapest, which is one of the great capitals of Europe. It has thermal baths fed by hot springs, a hilltop castle and grand boulevards, and a dining and nightlife scene that includes the famous ruin bars. But beyond the capital, Hungary has medieval towns, baroque wine regions, the biggest lake in Central Europe, folk traditions on the puszta plains and a thousand years of history.

It is also excellent value, with train and bus links that reach nearly everywhere, comfortable hotels, and food and wine that cost far less than in Austria next door. English is widely spoken by younger people in Budapest, and less so in the countryside. The best months are April to June and September to October.
placesIntro: Ordered roughly by how strongly we would recommend each for a first visit. Budapest is the essential; the Danube Bend, Eger and Lake Balaton add variety, and the others reward those with more time.
thingsToDoIntro: The experiences that recur across the country and make a Hungarian trip feel like one.

thingsToDo.title: Soak in a thermal bath
thingsToDo.text: Hungary sits on hot springs, and its baths are part of daily life, from the palatial Széchenyi in Budapest to small spa towns. See [[budapest|Budapest]].
thingsToDo.tip: Bring flip-flops, a towel and a swimsuit, or rent them.

thingsToDo.title: Cruise the Danube
thingsToDo.text: The river passes Parliament and Buda Castle, and reaches the Danube Bend. See [[budapest|Budapest]] and [[danube-bend|the Danube Bend]].
thingsToDo.tip: Go at night for the lit-up views.

thingsToDo.title: Drink in a ruin bar
thingsToDo.text: Budapest's bars in derelict buildings are eclectic and lively. See [[budapest|Budapest]].
thingsToDo.tip: Go on weekday evenings for elbow room.

thingsToDo.title: Taste Tokaji wine
thingsToDo.text: The sweet Tokaji Aszú has been called the wine of kings. See [[tokaj|Tokaj]].

thingsToDo.title: Ride on the puszta
thingsToDo.text: The great plains have horsemen, cattle and traditional farms. See [[hortobagy|Hortobágy]].
thingsToDo.tip: Go in summer for the horse shows.

thingsToDo.title: Relax at Lake Balaton
thingsToDo.text: Central Europe's largest lake has beaches, vineyards and a lively summer season. See [[lake-balaton|Lake Balaton]].
thingsToDo.tip: Visit in June or September to avoid crowds.

thingsToDo.title: Wander a medieval castle town
thingsToDo.text: Eger, Sopron and Visegrád have castles and walls. See [[eger|Eger]] and [[sopron|Sopron]].

foodIntro: Hungarian food is rich and paprika-red, with stews, dumplings, sausages and pastries, plus some of Europe's most underrated wines.

foods.text: A paprika-spiced soup or stew of beef, potatoes and vegetables, traditionally cooked in a cauldron by herdsmen.

practicalIntro: The essentials, current for 2026. Hungary is easy and safe, though language, currency and a few local scams are worth knowing.

practical.language: Hungarian (Magyar), unrelated to most European languages. English is widely spoken in Budapest and tourist areas, German is common in the west, and English is limited in rural areas.
practical.currency: Hungarian forint (HUF, Ft). Roughly 330–400 forints to the US dollar in recent years. Hungary is in the EU but not the eurozone, and some tourist places quote euro prices at poor rates.
practical.money: Cards are accepted almost everywhere in cities, and contactless payment is common. Use bank ATMs (OTP, K&H), decline dynamic currency conversion, and beware of currency exchange booths with poor rates. Carry some forints for markets and small towns.
practical.visa: Hungary is in the EU and the Schengen Area. Many nationalities, including the United Kingdom, United States, Canada and Australia, can stay up to 90 days in any 180 without a visa. The EU's ETIAS authorisation has been planned, so check current rules.
practical.plugs: Type C and F (two round pins), 230 V, 50 Hz. UK and US visitors need an adaptor.
practical.tipping: About 10–15% in restaurants if a service charge is not already included. Check the bill, since many places add it.
practical.safety: Hungary is generally safe. Watch for pickpockets in Budapest's tourist areas and on public transport, and be wary of overpricing scams in some nightlife venues and unlicensed taxis. Use licensed taxis or apps such as Bolt and Főtaxi.
practical.connectivity: Very good. EU roaming applies to EU SIMs, and prepaid SIMs and eSIMs are cheap. Free Wi-Fi is common in cafés.
practical.timeZone: Central European Time, UTC+1, and UTC+2 in summer.

bestTime.headline: April–June and September–October
bestTime.summary: Hungary has a continental climate, with hot summers, cold winters, and pleasant springs and autumns.

seasons.text: Mild, green and less crowded, with blossom and outdoor terraces opening.
Hot, sometimes over 35°C. Lake Balaton is at its liveliest, and festivals fill Budapest.
Warm days, grape harvests and golden leaves, with lower prices.
Cold and grey, but Christmas markets and steaming outdoor baths are magical.

bestTime.avoid: July and August heatwaves in cities, and January and February for long sightseeing.

tripDuration.headline: 7–12 days for a first trip
tripDuration.summary: Hungary is small, and Budapest is the focus. A week covers the capital with a couple of day trips, and two weeks allows a loop through wine country and the south.

transport.intro: Trains and buses are cheap and cover the country. Budapest is the hub, and most journeys radiate from it.

options.text: InterCity trains link Budapest with Eger, Szeged, Pécs and Sopron in two to three hours. Book on the MÁV app.
options.detail: Cheap, though slower than in Western Europe.

options.text: Serve smaller towns and Lake Balaton.
Metro, trams and buses, with a 24- or 72-hour travel card.
Use Bolt or Főtaxi, and avoid street taxis.
Useful for Tokaj, Hortobágy and Hollókő. Motorways need an e-vignette, and the alcohol limit is zero.

culture.intro: Hungarians are proud, direct and hospitable, with a strong sense of history and a dry sense of humour. Family meals and toasts matter, and formal manners are appreciated in first meetings.

etiquette.title: Greet with a handshake
etiquette.text: Shake hands with everyone, including at the start and end of meetings.

etiquette.title: Avoid clinking beer glasses
etiquette.text: By tradition, Hungarians do not clink beer glasses, a custom linked to the 1849 revolution, though wine and spirits are fine.

etiquette.title: Use formal address
etiquette.text: Use titles and formal speech with strangers and elders.

etiquette.title: Bring a gift
etiquette.text: Flowers or wine if invited home.

etiquette.title: Remove your shoes
etiquette.text: In homes, guests are often offered slippers.

etiquette.title: Respect baths etiquette
etiquette.text: Shower before entering pools, and wear swim caps where required.

dos: Learn a few words: köszönöm (thank you), szia (hi), egészségedre (cheers)
Take a swim cap or rent one at some baths
Try pálinka, the local fruit brandy
Check the service charge on bills
donts: Don't exchange money on the street
Don't drink and drive, since the limit is zero
Don't compare Hungary to its neighbours

tipsIntro: The things that most often catch visitors out in Hungary, several of which are specific to how the country works.
tips: Use Bolt or Főtaxi instead of hailing taxis.
Decline currency conversion on card machines, and pay in forints.
Validate metro and tram tickets before boarding.
Book Széchenyi Baths and the Parliament tour in advance.
Check the service charge before adding a tip.
Buy an e-vignette before driving on motorways.
Bring cash for small towns and markets.
Watch for pickpockets on trams and in Váci Street.

faq.a: Yes, generally very safe. Watch for pickpockets and overpricing in tourist bars.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Hungary?
faq.a: Three to four days for Budapest, and ten to fourteen for a wider trip.
Yes, compared with Western Europe, and Budapest is very good value.

faq.q: What is the best time to visit Hungary?
faq.a: April to June and September to October.

faq.q: Do I need a visa for Hungary?
faq.a: Many nationalities can visit visa-free for 90 days under Schengen rules. Check current rules, including ETIAS.

faq.q: Can I use euros in Hungary?
faq.a: Some places accept euros but at poor rates. Use forints.
